questions.q: Identify the narrative perspective used in "कंकाल में टमाटर की खेती" and name the protagonist.
questions.a: The story uses first-person narrative perspective ("मैं" voice). The protagonist is the narrator himself — Izzat Tiskh reflecting on his childhood in Kankal. A wrong answer (e.g., "third person" or naming a villager as protagonist) reveals the student hasn't distinguished between the author and the narrative persona, or hasn't recognized the memoir structure where the writer becomes the central character.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the narrator says "वीक एंड्स पर शहरी भीड़ से पिकनिक मनाने वाले पहाड़ को जंगल समझ लेते हैं" and what this reveals about his character.
questions.a: The narrator critiques urban tourists who mistake a degraded, picnic-spot hill for a real forest — exposing their ecological illiteracy. This reveals his character as: (1) observant — he sees what casual visitors miss; (2) protective — he resents the trivialization of his homeland; (3) authoritative — his childhood intimacy grants him epistemic authority over outsiders. A wrong answer focusing only on "tourists are bad" misses the protagonist's self-positioning as a keeper of ecological memory.

questions.q: Apply the "Show, Don't Tell" principle: Find ONE sentence where the narrator SHOWS his grief through sensory detail rather than naming the emotion. Quote it and explain the effect.
questions.a: Sentence: "बांज के छांह से उतरते हुए गर्मियों में भी ठंडक का अहसास होता था... अब वह छांह नहीं रही।" (Paraphrased from text: the coolness under oak shade in summers is gone). Effect: The vanished sensory experience (coolth) makes grief tangible without using words like "dukh" or "vyatha." A student who quotes "मुझे बहुत दुख हुआ" fails the task — they've confused telling with showing, missing the writer's craft.

questions.q: Analyze the protagonist's relationship with his mother as revealed in the episode where she says "इस्स से मकान बनेंगे।" How does this micro-interaction reflect the macro conflict of the chapter?
questions.a: The mother's pragmatic acceptance ("houses will be built from this") contrasts with the narrator's horror at quarrying. She represents survival needs of the present; he represents ecological memory of the past. This mirrors the chapter's central tension: local livelihood vs. long-term ecological collapse. The protagonist doesn't demonize her — he understands ("हमारे वर्तमान के बाथफूज...") — showing his character as compassionate but uncompromising on principle. A wrong answer that calls the mother "greedy" or the narrator "privileged" flattens the moral complexity the text carefully builds.

questions.q: Evaluate: Is the narrator a reliable witness to environmental change? Support your judgment with two pieces of evidence from the text.
questions.a: Yes, he is reliable because: (1) He provides specific, verifiable data — "128 वर्षों में एक ही वर्ष 1899 था जब 15-75 इंच वर्षा हुई" and "1973 में 77 इंच वर्षा" — grounding memory in meteorological record. (2) He admits uncertainty: "फिर भी पहाड़ के लोग... कहते हैं कि तब भी खाना-पीना ठीक था" — acknowledging oral history's limits. A student claiming "he's biased because he's emotional" confuses subjectivity with unreliability; the text shows his emotion is evidence-based, not fantasy.

questions.q: Create a diary entry (80 words) from the protagonist's perspective on the night he realizes "हमारी थाती की तकनीकी क्षमता पहाड़ की विलक्षणता है" — capturing his intellectual awakening and emotional rupture.
questions.a: A strong entry will: (a) use first-person reflective voice; (b) reference the specific phrase or its meaning (traditional knowledge as hill-specific technology); (c) show the shift from nostalgia to analysis; (d) end with a resolve to document/resist. Example opening: "आज समझ आया — हमारे बुजुर्गों का 'पत्थर जोड़ना' कोई पिछड़ापन नहीं, पहाड़ की गुरुत्वाकर्षण से लड़ाई थी।" A weak entry stays in nostalgia ("मुझे बचपन याद आया") without the conceptual leap the text demands.
